BestWonders of the World

Ancient wonders, natural marvels and modern feats of engineering across every continent. Several of the most famous are now far more managed than their photographs suggest — timed tickets, one-way routes, roped distances and daily caps are normal at the top of this list, and the picture you have in mind was usually taken before any of that existed.

Great Barrier Reef
Queensland, Australia
New Seven Wonders of NatureUNESCO World Heritage
The world's largest coral reef system, stretching 2,300 kilometres along Australia's northeast coast and comprising over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands. Visible from space, it supports an extraordinary marine ecosystem including 1,500 fish species, 4,000 mollusc species, and 30 whale and dolphin species. Snorkelling and diving from Cairns and the Whitsundays are the principal visitor entry points.

Angkor Wat
Siem Reap, Cambodia
UNESCO World HeritageLargest Religious Monument
The largest religious monument ever built, constructed in the first half of the 12th century as a Hindu temple for the Khmer Empire and gradually converted to Buddhism by the late 12th century. The complex covers roughly 400 acres and is surrounded by a moat 190 meters wide. The five central towers represent Mount Meru, home of the gods; the bas-relief galleries running the full perimeter of the outer walls depict scenes from Hindu mythology and Khmer history at a scale and precision not matched in the ancient world. The site is reached from Siem Reap, about six kilometers away.

Easter Island (Rapa Nui)
Valparaíso Region, Chile
UNESCO World HeritageNew Seven Wonders of Nature Candidate
A remote volcanic island in the southeastern Pacific, famous for nearly 1,000 monolithic stone statues called moai carved by the Rapa Nui people between roughly 1250 and 1500. The moai — the largest weighing 82 tonnes — were quarried at Rano Raraku and transported across the island using methods still debated. The island is 3,700 kilometres west of continental Chile and reached by regular flights from Santiago.

Mount Everest
Solukhumbu District, Nepal
World's Highest Peak — 8,849 mNew Seven Wonders of Nature
At 8,849 metres, the highest point on Earth, straddling the Nepal–Tibet border in the Himalaya. The summit was first reached by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay in 1953. Most expeditions approach from the Nepal side via Everest Base Camp (5,364 m), reached by a 12-day trek from Lukla. Trekking to Base Camp requires no technical climbing; summiting requires extreme mountaineering experience, months of acclimatisation, and a Nepal government permit.

Stonehenge
Wiltshire, England
UNESCO World HeritageBuilt c. 3000–1500 BC
A prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain, constructed and modified over roughly 1,500 years beginning around 3000 BC. The massive sarsen stones — some weighing 25 tonnes — were transported from Marlborough Downs 25 kilometres away; the smaller bluestones came from Wales, 250 kilometres distant. The site is aligned with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. English Heritage manages the monument; timed tickets are required and inner access at ground level is restricted to solstice openings.
Wikipedia UNESCO English Heritage Map
Grand Canyon
Arizona, United States
UNESCO World Heritage1.6 Billion Years of Geology
A gorge carved by the Colorado River over five to six million years, 446 kilometers long, up to 29 kilometers wide, and over 1,800 meters deep. The exposed rock layers read back 1.6 billion years of Earth's geological history in striped bands of red, orange, and cream. The South Rim — open year-round — sits at roughly 2,100 meters elevation and holds the main visitor facilities. The North Rim, 350 meters higher, is open only mid-May through mid-October and reached by a 340-kilometer road from the South Rim. The inner canyon floor, accessible by trail or mule, is a different climate and ecosystem from the rim above it.

Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya)
Zimbabwe / Zambia border
UNESCO World HeritageLargest Waterfall by Width and Flow
At 1,708 metres wide and 108 metres high, the largest waterfall in the world by combined width and flow, formed where the Zambezi River plunges into a narrow basalt gorge. Known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya — "The Smoke That Thunders" — the spray rises 400 metres and is visible 50 kilometres away. The falls are accessible from Victoria Falls town (Zimbabwe) and Livingstone (Zambia), both within walking distance of the main viewpoints and connected by a historic iron bridge over the gorge.
